# Fundamental-cell cap identities and exact signed-flux obstructions

This note retains the original integer lattice. It gives exact averaging
and signed sampling identities, then exhibits their nonzero errors at
actual deepest caps and exact depth-region facet certificates. It does
not claim a lower bound for OC or a minimizer classification.

The archived lattice-free-container notes already rule out unrestricted
volume attainment and certain facet-budget inequalities. The identities
and calibrations here concern a different issue: replacing mixed cap
fractions by ambient cap fractions through fundamental-cell averaging.

## 1. Exact fundamental-cell averaging, with the necessary weights

Let A be a bounded Borel subset of R^n times R^d and let

    M_t(A)=sum_(z in Z^n) vol_d(A_(z+t)), t in [0,1)^n.

Tonelli and the disjoint half-open unit-cell partition give exactly

    integral_[0,1)^n M_t(A) dt=vol_(n+d)(A).           (1)

This includes d=0, with counting measure on zero-dimensional fibers.
For a convex body C and a closed ambient halfspace H, put M_t=M_t(C)
and p_t(H)=M_t(C intersect H)/M_t when M_t>0, and put p_t=0 otherwise.
Then

    integral M_t p_t(H) dt / integral M_t dt
       = vol(C intersect H)/vol(C).                  (2)

It is the MASS-WEIGHTED phase average, not the unweighted average of
p_t, that equals the ambient fraction. No statement at the specified
phase t=0 follows from this identity. For finitely many caps H_j and
real coefficients c_j, it also gives the signed identity

    integral M_t sum_j c_j[p_0(H_j)-p_t(H_j)] dt
      = vol(C) sum_j c_j p_0(H_j)
          -sum_j c_j vol(C intersect H_j),           (3)

provided M_0>0. All sums are finite. Normals, including oblique ones,
are kept unchanged in this calculation.

## 2. One integer variable: a signed Euler identity with boundary mass

Suppose A is a full-dimensional convex body in R times R^d, d>=1,
with projection [a,b], a<b. Put f(t)=vol_d(A_t) on [a,b], and extend
f to be zero outside. The section-volume function is continuous on
[a,b] and absolutely continuous there. One direct justification is as
follows. Convex interpolation with a fixed interior section proves
Hausdorff convergence to either endpoint section, while compactness
gives the opposite Hausdorff inclusion. Volume is continuous for
compact convex sections. Brunn--Minkowski makes f^(1/d) a nonnegative
concave function on [a,b]. A continuous concave function is absolutely
continuous: its monotone one-sided derivatives integrate to its
increments on interior compact intervals, and monotone convergence
on either side of its maximum extends this to the endpoints. Composing
with the bounded C1 function r -> r^d preserves absolute continuity.

Define the centered sawtooth

    B(t)=t-floor(t)-1/2 if t is not an integer,
    B(t)=0 if t is an integer.

Its distributional derivative is dt-sum_(k in Z) delta_k. The
distributional derivative of the extended f is

    Df=f'(t)1_(a,b)dt+f(a)delta_a-f(b)delta_b.

Then the EXACT CLOSED-fiber sum is

    sum_(k in Z) f(k)
      = integral f(t)dt + integral B(t)dDf(t)
          + (1/2)1_(a in Z)f(a)
          + (1/2)1_(b in Z)f(b).                     (4)

To prove (4), integrate B f' on each open interval between consecutive
integers in (a,b). Since B'=1 there, ordinary integration by parts
applies. The jump from the left value 1/2 to the right value -1/2
contributes exactly f(k) at every interior integer k. At a noninteger
endpoint the remaining terms are B(a)f(a)-B(b)f(b). At an integer
endpoint the one-sided integration gives half its fiber value; the
last two terms of (4) supply the other half required by a CLOSED
section. This proves the identity, including both endpoint conventions.

For d=0 the same proof applies to an interval with f=1 on [a,b].
No f^(1/d) notation is needed in that case.

For a full-dimensional polytope A, (4) has a boundary-flux form. Let
N_z denote the integer-coordinate component of its outward unit normal.
Then

    M_0(A)=vol(A)-integral_(boundary A) B(z)N_z dH_d
             +(1/2)1_(a in Z)vol_d(A_a)
             +(1/2)1_(b in Z)vol_d(A_b).             (5)

For a smooth compactly supported test g, the divergence theorem gives
integral_(boundary A)g(z)N_z dH_d=integral f(z)g'(z)dz
=-integral g dDf. Approximate B on a fixed bounded interval by symmetric
smoothings; their values at an integer tend to zero, their absolute
values are uniformly bounded, and elsewhere they tend to B. Dominated
convergence for the finite boundary measure and the finite measure |Df|
proves (5). This supplies the claimed discontinuous test legitimately.

Apply (4), or (5) for polytopes, to A=C intersect H whenever it has
full ambient dimension. If it is lower-dimensional but has positive
d-dimensional mixed volume, convexity forces it to lie in one vertical
hyperplane z=a, and its contribution is exactly
1_(a in Z)vol_d(A_a). In every other lower-dimensional case all d-volume
fibers vanish. Thus a supporting cap carrying an entire boundary fiber
is treated separately, rather than being lost in a surface integral.

## 3. Canonical-body obstruction at an actual deepest OBLIQUE cap

Let n=1,d=2, L>1, and in continuous coordinates (x,y) put

    A=[-L,L] times [-1,1],
    B=[-2,-1] times [-L,L],
    C=conv(({0} times A) union ({1} times B)).

Its only integer fibers are exactly A and B, and C=conv(S). At real
0<=z<=1 its section is the rectangle

    x in [-L(1-z)-2z, L(1-z)-z],
    y in [-(1-z)-Lz, (1-z)+Lz].                      (6)

The mixed total mass is 4L+2L=6L. At an extreme integer base, any
within-fiber halfspace can be extended with a sufficiently large
integer-coordinate tilt to exclude the other bounded fiber. Conversely
every containing ambient halfspace contains a within-fiber halfspace
through the point. Hence its raw mixed depth equals its raw ordinary
fiber depth. A rectangle has maximum raw depth half its area, attained
at its center: central symmetry proves the lower bound, and the smaller
of opposite through-point halves proves the upper bound. Therefore

    max_(w in S) depth_S(w)=1/3,

and (0,0,0) is an actual global maximizer.

The oblique closed cap H={x+z>=0} is an actual minimizing cap there.
It captures half of A and only the zero-area supporting edge x=-1 of B.
Consequently M_0(C intersect H)/M_0(C)=1/3.

In (6), its retained x-width is exactly L(1-z), so direct integration
gives

    vol_3(C)=(2L^2+6L+1)/3,
    vol_3(C intersect H)=L(L+2)/3,
    vol_3(C intersect H)/vol_3(C)-1/3
       =(L^2-1)/[3(2L^2+6L+1)]>0.                  (7)

For the rational choice L=2 the ambient ratio is 8/21, the mixed ratio
is 1/3, and their difference is 1/21. The opposite continuous cap
H'={-x-2z>=0} has the same two ratios; its continuous normal balances
that of H. Thus even this positive circuit has a strictly signed
sampling correction. Its projected contact is z=0; no lattice-free
positive-level conclusion is asserted from that single circuit.

This example rules out a nonnegative signed correction at an active
deepest cap even after replacing the body by its canonical hull conv(S).
It does not certify an extremum over bodies or a below-OC budget.

## 4. Equal-budget exact lattice-free depth facets do not cancel the error

Now take n=d=1 and the rational triangle

    C=conv{(-1/2,-1),(3/2,-1),(1/2,3)}.

Its only integer fibers are S_0=S_1=[-1,1], both strictly inside the
projection interval. Thus M_0(C)=4 and vol_2(C)=4. Its section roof is
4z+1 for z<=1/2 and 5-4z for z>=1/2, and its floor is -1.

We first compute the exact projected depth profile of this S. Reflection
in x=0 preserves the measure. Convexity of depth upper-level sets gives
that at every real z the point (z,0) maximizes depth in its vertical line.
For 0<=z<=1/2, a cap through (z,0) of positive continuous coefficient
can be written x>=a(t-z), with t the base coordinate. Put
L(c)=min(2,max(0,1-c)). Its raw mass is

    L(-az)+L(a(1-z)).

For a>=0 this decreases from 2 to 1/(1-z) until a=1/(1-z), then
increases until it reaches 2; if z=0 the minimum remains 1 for larger
a. For a<=0 it is at least 2: before either clipping it is
2+|a|(1-2z), and while one summand is clipped at 2 the other is
nonnegative. Vertical caps have mass at least 2 at these points.
Reflection in t=1/2 handles the remaining z. Thus

    g(z):=max_x depth_S(z,x)=1/[4 max(z,1-z)], 0<=z<=1.
                                                               (8)

Shrinking any containing cap to the point justifies taking through-point
caps in this minimization. The usual closed-halfspace definition is used
throughout; all nonvertical boundaries have mixed measure zero here.

Consequently the depth region at level 1/3 has projection exactly
[1/4,3/4]. Consider its four supporting caps

    H_1^+={ x-(4/3)z>=-1/3},
    H_1^-={-x-(4/3)z>=-1/3},
    H_2^+={ x+(4/3)z>=1},
    H_2^-={-x+(4/3)z>=1}.                            (9)

Every cap in (9) has raw mixed mass 4/3 and normalized mass 1/3.
Their full ambient normals sum to zero. Within either group their
continuous normals form a positive balanced pair. The first group's
two hyperplanes meet at (1/4,0), the second at (3/4,0); these points
belong to the actual depth region by (8), and to C. The complementary
inequalities define a rhombus with projection [1/4,3/4], so it is a
bounded closed mixed-lattice-free container. A point strictly on the
cap side of any plane has depth below 1/3 by moving that plane slightly
past it. Thus the asserted contacts are actual supporting contacts,
not arbitrary auxiliary contacts.

Exact polygon areas, however, are

    vol(C intersect H_1^+)=vol(C intersect H_2^+)=2,
    vol(C intersect H_1^-)=vol(C intersect H_2^-)=9/8.  (10)

For example the first positive cap is the triangle with vertices
(-1/2,-1),(1,1),(1/2,3); the first negative cap is the triangle with
vertices (-1/2,-1),(1,-1),(-1/8,1/2). Reflection in z=1/2 gives the
other two areas. Hence

    sum_j p_0(H_j)=4/3,
    sum_j vol(C intersect H_j)/vol(C)=25/16,
    their signed difference=-11/48.                  (11)

Equivalently the right side of the exact phase identity (3), with
c_j=1, is -11/12. All endpoint fibers of these four cap polygons have
zero length, so (5) has no endpoint correction for them. Their total
sawtooth boundary flux is therefore +11/12, although all full normals
balance, all mixed budgets coincide, and all lattice-free depth-facet
contacts are attained. No cancellation or favorable sign follows from
those hypotheses alone.

## 5. Fixed mixed data can coexist with nearly full ambient cap mass

For any rational R>2 put

    C_R=conv{(-1/(R-1),-1),(1+1/(R-1),-1),(1/2,R)}.

The same two integer fibers [-1,1] remain unchanged and lie inside the
projection. Thus the entire mixed depth function and every depth-region
certificate above remain unchanged. The closed cap H={x>=z} has mixed
fraction 1/4, attained at the globally deepest point (0,0).
Direct triangle areas give

    vol(C_R)=(R+1)^2/[2(R-1)],
    vol(C_R intersect H)=(R-1)(2R-1)/[2(2R-3)],
    vol(C_R intersect H)/vol(C_R)
      =(R-1)^2(2R-1)/[(2R-3)(R+1)^2] -> 1.           (12)

The cap's lower-left intersection is
(-1/(2R-3),-1/(2R-3)); its other section endpoint is (1,1).
These determine (12) together with the apex.

This last freedom disappears if one first insists on C=conv(S).
Section 3 separately proves that even canonicalization does not provide
a universally favorable sampling sign. The exact depth-facet example
has level 1/3 above its actual maximum mixed depth 1/4; it is not a
counterexample to OC and is not asserted to arise from a bad minimum.
